signals.title: The Storyteller in the Model: Narrative Pattern Inheritance, Escalation Dynamics, and Alignment Governance in LLMs
signals.summary: LLMs are trained predominantly on human-authored text, yet the structural and narrative conventions embedded in that text are rarely examined as a source of systematic behavioral influence, or as a governance risk in deployed systems. This paper considers whether the storytelling patterns inherent in published human writing, including archetypal roles such as protagonist, antagonist, and underdog, as well as tension-and-resolution narrative arcs, are absorbed during training and subsequently surface in LLM outputs, causing responses to drift toward unexpected, adversarial, or rhetorically enticing behaviors over extended interactions.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments. Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators. High relevance to C2A2 operations; include in next leadership brief.
signals.long_summary: This paper investigates how large language models (LLMs), primarily trained on human-written text, may inherit and reproduce structural and narrative conventions found in that text. It emphasizes that the storytelling patterns, such as archetypal roles like protagonist and antagonist, and typical narrative arcs, might influence LLM behavior in ways that lead to unexpected, adversarial, or persuasive responses over time. The study raises important questions about the implications of these narrative patterns as potential governance risks in real-world applications of LLMs. Understanding these effects is crucial for creating safer and more aligned AI systems, particularly for professionals engaged in AI ethics and governance. This matters for the community keeping up with AI as it highlights the need for careful oversight and understanding of how narratives shape AI interactions and potential risks.

signals.title: Distinguishing Artificial from Authentic: Evaluating LLMs for Detecting LLM-Generated Content
signals.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by students to generate natural language responses and program code, there is growing interest in whether LLMs themselves can be used to distinguish AI-generated work from human-authored submissions. In this paper, we investigate the extent to which LLMs can detect their own generated content across multiple educational task types, including programming exercises, reflective writing, and short-answer questions.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: This paper explores the ability of large language models (LLMs) to identify content they have generated, particularly in educational settings where students use these models to create responses and code. It examines how effectively LLMs can discern AI-generated work from human-generated submissions across various tasks like programming exercises, reflective writing, and short-answer questions. As the integration of AI into educational environments grows, understanding LLMs' detection capabilities becomes crucial for maintaining academic integrity and fostering appropriate usage of these technologies among students. This discussion is significant for a community engaged in AI, as it emphasizes the balance between innovation and ethical considerations in education.

signals.title: SCoPE: Shift-Aware Speaker-Conditioned Priors for Emotion Recognition in Conversations
signals.summary: In conversations, human emotions are transient; however, they tend to persist across multiple utterances. For example, we rarely switch instantly between contrasting emotions such as happiness and anger.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments. Monitor adoption pressure and revise formation cadence for tool onboarding.
signals.long_summary: The abstract discusses the nature of human emotions in conversations, emphasizing that while emotions can be transient, they often persist across multiple utterances. This persistence means that it is uncommon for individuals to switch abruptly between opposing emotions like happiness and anger. This understanding of emotional continuity in dialogue is essential for improving emotion recognition systems in AI. Recognizing these patterns in conversations is crucial for developing more effective AI that can understand and respond appropriately to human emotions, which is increasingly important in various applications of AI in communication platforms.
